newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs begin 11th-hour election campaign in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Serbs begin 11th-hour election campaign in Croatia.

text.p: Serb politicians on Thursday kicked off a grudging, last-minute campaign for regional elections that will lead to the re-integration of a breakaway enclave in Croatia.

As Eastern Slavonia's Serbs unveiled a platform for strong minority rights in lieu of the outright independence for which they once waged war, U.N. transitional authorities voiced optimism about the dawn of democracy in the region.
"I am very pleased...and excited about the beginning of a democratic process here," U.S. diplomat Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES), told Reuters.
Eastern Slavonia was one of three Serb minority regions that rebelled against Croatia's move to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991 and proclaimed their own state.

Croatia recaptured two enclaves in blitz offensives two years ago, prompting Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, a fertile, oil-producing strip on the Danube River border with Serbia, to accept a gradual, peaceful return to Croatian rule.

In anticipation of April 13 regional elections to be held across Croatia, local Serb factions shelved differences and united "to protect Serb interests" with a single party (SDSS) registered minutes before the deadline expired on Tuesday.

Croatia has promised significant minority rights for local Serbs, proclaimed a general amnesty for all who joined the 1991 revolt and issued citizenship documents to Serb applicants which must be presented at polling stations.
But Croatia also made a list of 150 names of un-amnestied war-crimes suspects whom it wants to see in court.

The SDSS launched its campaign on Thursday with a low-key news conference in the enclave's war-shattered main town, Vukovar, attended by a few Croatian journalists, something unthinkable just a few months ago.

"We were late in registering, we had problems because some of our candidates do not have Croatian papers while others are on Croatia's wanted list," said Vojislav Stanimirovic, the relatively moderate leader of the SDSS. "But it is clear to us (now) that only by political means can we keep fighting."
The wanted list is one of the most controversial issues. Although it has been greatly reduced under Western pressure for Croatian-Serb reconciliation, the Serbs still challenge it.
"We'll ask for international arbitration in this matter so Croatian and international judges can hear the suspects' testimonies," Stanimirovic said.

Fear and uncertainty remain the predominant feeling in the area. At least 20 percent of its estimated 120,000 Serbs will probably flee reintegration to Serbia but the majority now have obtained Croatian citizenship documents.
"Now most people want to stay after the election and see how good or bad it is," UNTAES spokesman Philip Arnold said.
About half the Serbs are refugees from elsewhere and many will soon have to yield housing to original owners -- 80,000 Croat refugees who formed the regional majority before 1991.
"I live in a Croatian house now so I will have to move out," said Anka Mrkela, 39, a Serb refugee whose home in the western town of Benkovac was burnt by Croatian troops in 1995.

"I'll vote to exercise my rights but I don't think I'll ever return to Benkovac, much as I want to," she told Reuters while queueing at a Croatian documentation office. "I will stay here if I find somewhere to live."
The vote is expected to split along strict communal lines -- Serbs for Stanimirovic's new party and Croats primarily for the nationalist HDZ of President Franjo Tudjman.

Klein said Croatian state institutions would be phased in steadily over a three-month period after the elections, setting the stage for a return of all displaced people -- the ultimate goal of the UNTAES mandate.
"But it takes money -- to rebuild infrastructure and economy -- and Croatia doesn't have that money.
"So the key is the international community. But in order to ask them for resources all refugees, Croats and Serbs, will have to work together," Klein said.
